extracted.intended_audience: academics and researchers in public administration, political science, and algorithmic decision-making (study authors/readers interested in automation bias and discrimination)
extracted.subtask_description: Vignette-style survey experiments in the Netherlands where participants act as school-board members deciding teacher employment, used to test automation bias and selective adherence to algorithmic versus human advice. Includes preregistration, randomized manipulations, attention/manipulation checks, exclusion rules, and logistic-regression analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preregistration
rubrics_metrics.description: The studies were preregistered and the preregistration forms are available (study 1: https://aspredicted.org/5de9d.pdf; study 2: https://aspredicted.org/v3u29.pdf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological choices are further discussed in supplementary section A6. Preregistration supports directional hypotheses and informs reporting (one-sided p values are additionally reported for preregistered directional hypotheses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment and sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants recruited through large online panel companies (Dynata for studies 1 and 2; ICTU/Flitspanel for study 3). Sample sizes: study 1 N=605, study 2 N=904, pooled N=1,509, study 3 invited 3,294 with 1,345 completions (41% response).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report sample characteristics and compare to target population (e.g., average age and education comparable to Dutch civil servants, over-/under-representation noted). Use panel details and response rates in interpretation of generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey language and contextual tailoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys were conducted in Dutch and the experimental design was tailored to the Dutch context (all schools operate under publicly funded educational associations; participants act as board members of a hypothetical Dutch high-school).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual tailoring ensures ecological validity; report local institutional features that shape task realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental task (vignette role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants act as board members deciding employment for three new teachers; only two can be permanently hired, so participants choose one teacher whose contract will not be renewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear role and decision problem to participants to simulate real-world decision making; include full survey instrument in supplements (A8 and A9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Information presented per subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Each teacher is presented with two inputs: a brief qualitative HR evaluation and a numeric prediction score (ILE evaluation score) ranging from 1 to 10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make both qualitative and quantitative inputs explicit and visible to participants; design numeric scale to resemble real-world risk/prediction scores (e.g., COMPAS-like 1–10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice source manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents are randomly assigned to be told that the ILE score is produced either by a machine learning algorithm (algorithmic advice) or by consultants/human experts (human-expert advice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly label the source of numeric predictions to participants; use equal framing across conditions aside from source to isolate source effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolstering predictive credibility equally across conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: To bolster confidence in ILE, participants in both conditions are told it 'has proven highly effective in predicting teacher performance, with an accuracy rate of 95%.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide identical credibility statements across advice-source conditions to avoid confounding perceived accuracy with source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate incongruence design
rubrics_metrics.description: Task deliberately creates incongruence between the numeric ILE score and the qualitative HR evaluation: the lowest ILE score (4) is never matched with the most negative qualitative evaluation. Two incongruence levels are used: high incongruence (lowest ILE paired with most favorable qualitative eval) and modest incongruence (lowest ILE paired with mixed qualitative eval).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use systematic mismatch to test whether participants follow numeric advice despite contradictory qualitative evidence; randomize incongruence condition across respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomization of score distribution and order
rubrics_metrics.description: For exploratory purposes the distribution of ILE scores (4, 6, 8) was randomized across the three teachers and the order of teachers was randomized (except study 2 where order was not randomized based on study 1 results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomize assignment of scores/positions to mitigate ordering and position effects; report when randomization was omitted and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimizing subject characteristic confounds
rubrics_metrics.description: All three teachers are female, have typical Dutch names, and teach natural sciences to minimize other characteristics that might affect decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardize non-manipulated attributes across vignette subjects to isolate experimental manipulations; report choices and rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnicity/name manipulation for stereotype tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Study 2 manipulates the surname of the teacher who receives lowest ILE (control: typical Dutch names; treatment: change to 'El Amrani' to signal Moroccan-Dutch background) to test selective adherence aligned with stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select real-world salient cues for ethnicity; restrict certain analyses to respondents for whom stereotype effects are theorized (e.g., respondents of Dutch descent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome variable coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Main outcome is participants' likelihood to follow the ILE score; coded binary with 1 when participants chose to fire the teacher with the lowest ILE score and 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, pre-specified binary coding for primary outcome and report it consistently across analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow-up questions confirm participants' awareness of the source of advice (algorithmic vs human) and of the actual ILE score (reported in supplementary section A3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include manipulation checks to verify participants perceived experimental stimuli as intended; report rates of successful checks and use them in robustness analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention checks and minimum completion time filters
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys included an attention check; participants who did not pass the attention check or completed the questionnaire in under 3 minutes were excluded from analyses (studies 1 & 2). Study 3 omitted an attention check at panel's request but excluded responses under 3 minutes (all participants completed in >3 minutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predefine attention and speed filters, verify that exclusion criteria are not associated with randomization, and report exclusions transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample restrictions for specific hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: For selective-adherence hypotheses involving ethnicity (H2, H3), analyses were filtered to include only respondents of Dutch descent (e.g., n=792 in study 2; n=1,203 in study 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict subsamples when theory predicts effects only among certain respondent groups; justify and document screening criteria and balance checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and covariate control
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomized groups are reported balanced on gender, reported income, education; slight age differences in one group were controlled for in robust analyses (supplementary table A1.1 etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report balance diagnostics and include covariates in robustness checks if needed; show that filtering/exclusions are unrelated to assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical modeling and reporting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use logistic regression models reporting odds ratios (OR), 95% confidence intervals, z statistics, and p values. Two-tailed p values are used uniformly for consistency; for preregistered directional hypotheses one-sided p values are additionally reported in tables and text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-specify statistical tests and p-value conventions; transparently report both two-sided default tests and any one-sided tests tied to preregistration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness checks and supplementary analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Robustness analyses include controlling for covariates, restricting samples to those who passed manipulation checks, pooling samples to increase power, testing interactions with demographic variables, checking different incongruence conditions, and filtering by respondents' familiarity with algorithm use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform and report multiple robustness checks to assess stability of findings; include supplementary tables (A5.x) documenting these analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power analysis and detectable effect reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Power calculations are reported: e.g., study 1 estimated modest effect size OR=1.5 detectable with power 0.8 (p=0.05 one-sided); pooled sample power and post hoc power discussion in supplementary section A7; study 3 sample size sufficient for detecting OR=1.52.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide pre-study power estimates for detectable effect sizes and discuss power limitations for interaction tests and null findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive and tabular reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Present descriptive distributions of choices by condition (Tables 2, 4, 6, 8) alongside regression results (Tables 1, 3, 5, 7, 9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both raw descriptive percentages and inferential model output to allow readers to assess practical magnitude and statistical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual sensitivity and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation of results accounts for broader contextual events (study 3 fieldwork occurred amid the Dutch 'childcare benefits scandal' involving algorithmic discrimination), and participants' familiarity with algorithm use affected responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report contemporaneous events and participants' reported familiarity as potential moderators; discuss how context may affect external validity and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design choice documentation and supplements
rubrics_metrics.description: Full survey instrument, supplementary tables, and methodological appendices (A2–A9, A5.x, A6, A7) are provided for transparency and detailed methodological choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide complete materials and supplementary analyses to allow replication and evaluation of design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of experimental cautions (ethical/fieldwork decisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers chose not to withhold fieldwork despite coinciding events (e.g., scandal) believing investigation under such conditions yields meaningful insights; they note this decision and its implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and justify any fieldwork continuation decisions when external events might bias responses; discuss implications for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding and specific stimulus parameterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific numeric ILE score values (4, 6, 8) and ensure the negative qualitative evaluation is never assigned to the lowest ILE (4); report how distribution/randomization of these scores was implemented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-specify numeric stimulus levels and their assignment rules to create intended incongruence structure; report randomization checks and explore different assignment permutations.
